Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh”

A **hillshade** layer is just a *paint* layer that turns the raw elevation values from a `raster-dem` source into a black-and-white relief image.  
If the result looks like:

* very dark shadows / very bright highlights  
* “chalky” or “blown-out” ridges  
* a flat-looking surface when you try to soften it by adding more hillshade layers  

…then the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of the following paint properties:

| Property | What it does | Typical harsh default |
|----------|--------------|-----------------------|
| `hillshade-method` | How the light is simulated. `standard` (default) uses a single light direction, which can give strong, high-contrast shadows. | `standard` |
| `hillshade-exaggeration` | Multiplies the slope before shading. Values > 0.5 make shadows deeper. | `0.5` |
| `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light (0-360°). Certain angles line up with map features and create strong bands. | `335°` |
| `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | The actual colors used for shadows/highlights. Opaque black / white give the highest contrast. | `#000000` / `#FFFFFF` |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the light follows the viewport (`viewport`) or the map (`map`). With `viewport` the light never rotates with the map, which can feel “flat” when you spin the map. | `viewport` |

### The easiest, most-effective fix: **use the new multi-directional method**

Since **MapLibre GL JS 5.5** you can replace a whole stack of manually-added hillshade layers with a **single** layer that does the same job (and far less work) by setting:

```json
"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"
```

`multidirectional` lights the terrain from several independent directions in one pass, which dramatically softens the contrast while keeping the relief visible.

### Full “soft-hillshade” recipe

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade-soft",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",          // your raster-dem source name
  "paint": {
    /* 1️⃣ Soften the shading */
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",

    /* 2️⃣ Reduce overall contrast (optional) */
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4,          // < 0.5 = softer shadows
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // light rotates with map bearing

    /* 3️⃣ Give shadows/highlights a little transparency */
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)",

    /* 4️⃣ (optional) tweak the light direction if you still want a dominant side */
    "hillshade-illumination-direction": 315   // any 0-360° you like
  }
}
```

#### What each line does

| Line | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` | Replaces the old “stack-several-layers-with-different-directions” trick with a single pass that blends light from many angles. |
| `"hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4` | Lowers the slope-amplification factor, making shadows less deep. |
| `"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"` | The light source now follows the map’s bearing, so rotating the map also rotates the light – a more natural look. |
| `"hillshade-shadow-color"` / `"hillshade-highlight-color"` | Using `rgba()` adds alpha, so shadows/highlights blend with the underlying imagery instead of completely covering it. |
| `"hillshade-illumination-direction": 315` | If you still want a primary light direction (e.g., from the northwest), set it here; otherwise you can omit it and let the multi-directional algorithm decide. |

### Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

| Pitfall | Why it happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Stacking several hillshade layers** | Before GL 5.5 people added 2-3 layers with different `hillshade-illumination-direction`s to fake multi-directional lighting. This doubles (or triples) draw calls and can still look harsh. | **Remove all extra hillshade layers** and keep only the one shown above. |
| **Leaving the default opaque colors** | `#000000` and `#FFFFFF` are fully opaque, so shadows/highlights completely overwrite the base map. | Use `rgba()` with an alpha of ~0.4-0.6 as in the example. |
| **Using `hillshade-exaggeration` > 1** | Exaggeration > 1 makes slopes look steeper, which intensifies shadows. | Keep it ≤ 0.5 for a gentle look; increase only if you really need dramatic relief. |
| **Forgetting the `raster-dem` source** | A hillshade layer must point at a **`raster-dem`** source, not a regular `raster` source. Otherwise you’ll just see the raw RGB DEM image. | Verify your source definition: `{ "type": "raster-dem", "url": "...", "encoding": "terrarium" }`. |
| **Running on an old MapLibre version** | `hillshade-method` and `multidirectional` were added in **v5.5**. Older builds will ignore the property and fall back to `standard`. | Upgrade to the latest MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.5) or at least 5.5.x. |

### Quick checklist to test your fix

1. **Upgrade** to the latest MapLibre GL JS (run `npm i maplibre-gl@latest` or pull the newest CDN script).  
2. **Replace** any existing hillshade layers with the single “soft” layer above.  
3. **Reload** the map and **pan/rotate** – you should see a smoother, less-contrasty relief.  
4. If it still feels too flat, increase `hillshade-exaggeration` a little (e.g., `0.5`) or adjust the `hillshade-illumination-direction`.  
5. If you want even more subtlety, lower the alpha values in the shadow/highlight colors (e.g., `rgba(30,40,80,0.3)`).

### Optional extra: combine hillshade with a color-relief layer

If you want a *colored* hypsometric tint **and** a soft hillshade, you can simply add a `color-relief` layer **below** the hillshade:

```json
{
  "id": "hypsometric",
  "type": "color-relief",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": {
    "color-relief-color": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["elevation"],
      0,   "#2c7bb6",
      500, "#abd9e9",
      1500,"#ffffbf",
      2500,"#fdae61",
      4000,"#ffffff"
    ],
    "color-relief-opacity": 0.7
  }
},
{
  "id": "hillshade-soft",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": { /* same paint as above */ }
}
```

The `color-relief` gives you a height-based palette, while the hillshade adds gentle shading on top.

---

#### TL;DR

* Use **one** hillshade layer.  
* Set `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` (GL 5.5+).  
* Lower `hillshade-exaggeration` (≈ 0.4).  
* Give shadows/highlights an `rgba()` color with some transparency.  
* Optionally set `hillshade-illumination-anchor` to `"map"` and tweak the direction.

That will turn a harsh, black-and-white relief into a smooth, natural-looking terrain overlay. Happy mapping!
